newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl investment drive raises little enthusiasm.
newsitem.headline: Kohl investment drive raises little enthusiasm.

text.p: A 25 billion mark ($14.7 billion) investment drive unveiled by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl has done little to excite economists or to placate the construction workers whose jobs it is intended to secure.

Despite Wednesday's announcement of the package by Kohl in Munich, several thousand builders continued their protests on Thursday in the streets of Berlin over what they see as a failure by the government and employers to tackle chronic unemployment in the industry.
Economists said the package, set to be approved next week, would not change their growth forecasts for 1997 and would make no real dent in Germany's post-war record unemployment of 4.7 million.
"The measures appear to be aimed at public opinion, showing people that the government is intent on doing something towards growth," Morgan Stanley economist Joachim Fels said.
Of the 25 billion marks, some 20 billion relate to cheap credits that will be available from institutions such as the Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau development agency.
"But there is no guarantee that these loans will be fully used. With interest rates at current low levels, the cost of borrowing is not so much of an issue among potential borrowers," Fels said.

The remaining five billion marks of accelerated public sector infrastructure investment would represent just 0.15 percent of gross domestic product even if, as is unlikely, it were to be released in the same year, he added.
Thomas Mayer, senior economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt, agreed that the measure would not alter the outlook for German growth this year, which the government has estimated at 2.5 percent.
"At most it reduces the downside risk on the growth forecast. Again, on unemployment (in the sector) it might just about do something to contain the increase," Mayer said.
Analysts said public construction investment in any case accounted for only a small proportion of overall construction spending. It was around 15 percent in 1995, the year of the most recent data.
"It is a very political measure -- particularly with the general elections coming up next year," Bayerische Vereinsbank analyst Christine Nestroy said.

Earlier this week, the ZDB building employers' federation said it expected overall building investment to fall a further 2.5 percent this year, continuing the steady decline seen since the heady years just after German reunification in 1990.

With a third of Germany's 1.3 million construction workers estimated to be without a job, pressure is mounting to find a solution to the problems in the industry, where fierce price competition has often cut profit margins to negligible levels.

As the protests continued in Berlin, building employers and trade union officials met in Frankfurt to seek agreement on a range of issues, including a new "bad weather" accord that unions hope will prevent the regular upsurge in unemployment that occurs each winter.
